motion-representations-s1.title: A car between two traffic lights
motion-representations-s1.text: A car pulls away from a red light, cruises, then brakes for the next light. The graph shows its velocity, with the direction of travel positive. Each part of the motion has a constant acceleration.

motion-representations-s2.title: Two runners on a straight path
motion-representations-s2.text: Runners A and B move along the same straight path. The graph shows each runner's position, measured from a lamppost, against time.

motion-representations-s3.title: A ball tossed up from a balcony
motion-representations-s3.text: A student on a balcony 15 m above the ground throws a ball straight up at 12 m/s. The ball rises, stops for an instant, then falls past the balcony to the ground. Air resistance is negligible. Take up as positive and g = 9.8 m/s².
motion-representations-s3.html: Key: gold arrow, the initial velocity; dashed line, the path of the ball.

motion-representations-s4.title: Stopping a car
motion-representations-s4.text: A car travels at 25 m/s on a straight road. The driver sees a stop sign, and 0.60 s later (the reaction time) starts braking. While braking, the car slows with a constant acceleration of −6.0 m/s² (forward is positive) until it stops.
motion-representations-s4.html: Key: gold arrow, velocity; the gray stretch is covered during the reaction time, the red stretch while braking.

items.q: What is the car's acceleration from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s?

mistakes.why: Value: 24 is the area under the graph, which is the displacement in meters. Acceleration is the slope.
Value: the slope is rise over run, Δv ÷ Δt, not Δt ÷ Δv.

why.correct: The acceleration is the slope of the v-t graph: (12 m/s − 0) ÷ (4.0 s − 0) = 3.0 m/s².

items.q: How far does the car travel from t = 0 to t = 14 s?

mistakes.why: Value: 168 m treats the car as moving at 12 m/s the whole time. The triangles at the start and end are only half as large as rectangles.
Value: 72 m is only the cruising part. Add the areas of the triangles for speeding up and slowing down.

why.correct: Displacement is the area under the v-t graph: triangle ½(4.0 s)(12 m/s) = 24 m, rectangle (6.0 s)(12 m/s) = 72 m, triangle ½(4.0 s)(12 m/s) = 24 m. Total = 120 m (two significant figures).

items.q: During which interval is the car's acceleration negative?
options: From 0 to 4 s
From 4 s to 10 s
At no time, since the velocity stays positive
From 10 s to 14 s

why.correct: Acceleration is the slope of the v-t graph. The slope is negative from 10 s to 14 s, while the car is still moving forward but slowing.
options: The graph rises there, so the slope is positive: the car speeds up.
The graph is flat there, so the slope is zero: steady velocity, no acceleration.
Velocity and acceleration have separate signs. The velocity is positive while it decreases, so a is negative.
Right: the v-t graph slopes downward there, so the slope (the acceleration) is negative.

items.q: Which describes the car's position-time graph from 10 s to 14 s?
options: Falling in a straight line
Rising and getting steeper
Rising but getting less steep, then level at 14 s
A horizontal line

why.correct: The slope of the x-t graph is the velocity. From 10 s to 14 s the velocity falls from 12 m/s to 0, so x keeps rising with a slope that decreases to zero.
options: A falling x-t graph means negative velocity; the car is still moving forward.
A steepening x-t graph means a growing velocity; here the velocity is shrinking.
Right: the velocity (the x-t slope) is positive and shrinking to zero, so x still increases, more and more slowly.
Horizontal means v = 0 for the whole interval; the car only stops at 14 s.

items.q: What is the car's average velocity for the whole 14 s?

mistakes.why: Value: 6.0 m/s averages the start and peak velocities, which only works for a single constant acceleration. Use total displacement ÷ total time.
Value: 12 m/s is the cruising speed. The car was slower than that while speeding up and slowing down.

why.correct: Average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 120 m ÷ 14 s = 8.6 m/s.

items.q: What is runner B's velocity?

mistakes.why: Value: 3.75 m/s divides B's final position by the time. B started at 10 m, so use the change in position: 30 − 10 = 20 m.

why.correct: Velocity is the slope of the x-t graph: (30 m − 10 m) ÷ (8.0 s − 0) = 2.5 m/s.

items.q: At t = 4.0 s, the two lines cross. What is true at that instant?
options: The runners have the same velocity
The runners are at the same position and have the same velocity
Runner B is just catching up to runner A
The runners are at the same position, but A is faster

why.correct: On an x-t graph, the height is the position and the slope is the velocity. Crossing lines share a position, not a velocity.
options: Equal velocity would mean equal slopes. The lines cross, which means equal positions.
The positions match, but the slopes (5.0 and 2.5 m/s) do not.
B started ahead at 10 m; it is A who catches up with B at 4.0 s.
Right: the crossing means equal x; A's line is steeper, so A has the larger velocity.

items.q: Which runner has the greater acceleration?
options: Runner A, because A's line is steeper
Runner B, because B started farther along
Neither; both accelerations are zero
Runner A, because A covers more distance

why.correct: Straight x-t lines mean constant velocities. A constant velocity means zero acceleration for both.
options: A steeper x-t line means a larger velocity, not an acceleration. A straight line has a constant velocity.
A starting position does not affect the acceleration.
Right: both x-t graphs are straight lines, so each runner's velocity is constant and neither accelerates.
More distance in the same time means a larger velocity, not an acceleration.

items.q: How far apart are the runners at t = 6.0 s?

mistakes.why: Value: 30 m is A's position. Subtract B's position, 25 m.

why.correct: Read the graph: A is at 30 m and B is at 25 m. Separation = 30 m − 25 m = 5.0 m.

items.q: Which describes the two runners' velocity-time graphs?
options: Two horizontal lines, A's higher than B's
Two lines crossing at t = 4.0 s
Two rising lines, A's steeper
A horizontal line for A and a rising line for B

why.correct: A straight x-t line has a constant slope, so its v-t graph is a horizontal line at that slope: 5.0 m/s for A, 2.5 m/s for B.
options: Right: each velocity is constant (5.0 and 2.5 m/s), so each v-t graph is flat, and A's is higher.
The x-t lines cross, but the velocities never become equal.
Rising v-t lines would mean speeding up; these runners keep a steady pace.
Both x-t graphs are straight, so both velocities are constant.

items.q: How long does the ball take to reach its highest point? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: 2.4 s is the time to rise and fall back to the balcony. The top is halfway, where v = 0.
Value: use v = v₀ + at with v = 0 at the top; the equation with t² is for a known displacement.

why.correct: At the top v = 0. Use v = v₀ + at with a = −9.8 m/s²: 0 = 12 m/s − (9.8 m/s²)t, so t = 12 ÷ 9.8 = 1.2 s.

items.q: How high above the balcony does the ball rise? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: 15 m forgets the 2 in v² = v₀² + 2aΔy. Δy = v₀²/(2g).
Value: the initial velocity must be squared: Δy = v₀²/(2g) = 144/19.6.

why.correct: With no time given, use v² = v₀² + 2aΔy: 0 = (12 m/s)² + 2(−9.8 m/s²)Δy, so Δy = 144 ÷ 19.6 = 7.3 m.

items.q: What is the ball's acceleration at its highest point?
options: Zero, because the ball is momentarily at rest
9.8 m/s² downward
9.8 m/s² upward, because the ball was thrown up
Smaller than 9.8 m/s², because the ball has slowed down

why.correct: Free fall means a = g downward at every point of the flight: on the way up, at the top and on the way down.
options: v = 0 is not a = 0: the velocity is changing from upward to downward at that instant.
Right: in free fall the acceleration is g downward the whole time, including the instant the velocity is zero.
The throw sets the initial velocity, not the acceleration; once released, the acceleration points down.
The acceleration does not depend on the speed; it stays 9.8 m/s² down throughout the flight.

items.q: As the ball falls back past the balcony, what is its velocity?
options: 12 m/s downward
12 m/s upward
Zero
24 m/s downward

why.correct: v² = v₀² + 2aΔy with Δy = 0 (back at the balcony) gives v² = v₀², so v = −12 m/s: the same speed, downward.
options: Right: with a constant acceleration, it loses 12 m/s on the way up and gains it back over the same distance down.
The speed is the same, but the ball is now moving down, so the velocity points down.
The velocity is zero only at the highest point.
Falling 7.3 m back to the balcony only restores the speed it lost rising 7.3 m: 12 m/s.

items.q: At what speed does the ball hit the ground, 15 m below the balcony? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: 17 m/s treats the ball as dropped from rest. It was thrown at 12 m/s, so v₀² = 144 m²/s² must be included.
Value: speeds do not add like that. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔy, which adds the squares.
Value: 438 is v², in m²/s². Take the square root.

why.correct: v² = v₀² + 2aΔy with v₀ = +12 m/s, a = −9.8 m/s², Δy = −15 m: v² = 144 + 294 = 438 m²/s², so the speed is √438 = 21 m/s.

items.q: How far does the car travel during the 0.60 s reaction time?

mistakes.why: Value: 7.5 m treats the car as slowing during the reaction time. It is not braking yet, so the velocity stays 25 m/s.

why.correct: Before braking the velocity is constant, so Δx = vt = (25 m/s)(0.60 s) = 15 m.

items.q: How far does the car travel while braking?

mistakes.why: Value: 104 m forgets the 2 in v² = v₀² + 2aΔx. Δx = v₀²/(2|a|).
Value: the initial velocity must be squared: (25 m/s)² = 625 m²/s².

why.correct: No time is given for braking, so use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx: 0 = (25 m/s)² + 2(−6.0 m/s²)Δx, so Δx = 625 ÷ 12 = 52 m.

items.q: How long does the braking last?

mistakes.why: Value: 4.8 s includes the reaction time. The question asks only about the braking.

items.q: The same car approaches at 1.5 times the speed with the same braking acceleration. How does its braking distance change?
options: It becomes 1.5 times as long
It becomes 3 times as long
It stays the same, because the braking is the same
It becomes 2.25 times as long

why.correct: From v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0: Δx = v₀²/(2|a|) ∝ v₀². Factor 1.5² = 2.25. (The reaction distance only grows by 1.5, since it is v₀t.)
options: That would hold if distance were proportional to v₀, but v₀ is squared.
Squaring 1.5 gives 2.25, not 2 × 1.5.
The car has more velocity to remove, so with the same acceleration it needs more distance.
Right: braking distance = v₀²/(2|a|), so it depends on v₀². 1.5² = 2.25.

items.q: Which velocity-time graph matches the car from the moment the driver sees the sign until it stops?
options: A straight line down from 25 m/s to zero, starting at t = 0
Flat at 25 m/s for 0.60 s, then a curve that gets steeper
Flat at 25 m/s for 0.60 s, then a straight line down to zero
Flat at 25 m/s for 0.60 s, then a drop straight down to zero

why.correct: Reaction: v constant, horizontal line. Braking: constant a, so a straight line with slope −6.0 m/s², reaching zero 4.2 s later.
options: This leaves out the reaction time, when the car has not started braking.
A constant acceleration gives a straight v-t line; a curve would mean the braking changes.
Right: constant velocity during the reaction time, then a constant negative slope (−6.0 m/s²) to v = 0.
A vertical drop would mean stopping in no time; braking takes 4.2 s.

items.q: A cart starts with a known velocity and speeds up with a known constant acceleration over a measured distance. The time is not known and not asked for. Which equation gives its final velocity most directly?
options: v = v₀ + at
v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀)
x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²
v(avg) = Δx/Δt

why.correct: Choose the equation that contains the unknown and the knowns and leaves out the quantity you do not have. Each constant-acceleration equation leaves out one quantity; v² = v₀² + 2aΔx leaves out t.
options: This needs the time, which is not known.
Right: it links v, v₀, a and the displacement without t.
This needs t, and it does not contain the final velocity.
This needs the time, and an average velocity is not the final velocity.

items.q: A stone dropped from rest takes 0.60 s to fall to the bottom of a dry well. How long would it take to fall from a height 4 times as great? Air resistance is negligible.

mistakes.why: Value: 2.4 s treats time as proportional to height. Height grows as t², so time grows as the square root of height.
Value: time grows as the square root of the height, not as its square.

why.correct: From rest, Δy = ½gt², so t = √(2Δy/g) ∝ √Δy. Four times the height gives √4 = 2 times the time: 1.2 s.

items.q: A sprinter leaves the blocks and her velocity-time graph curves: it rises steeply at first, then less and less steeply until it is flat. What does this show?
options: Her acceleration is constant until she reaches top speed
She slows down after the start
Her acceleration increases as she gets faster
Her acceleration is largest at the start and decreases to zero

why.correct: This is nonuniform acceleration, described from the graph only: the slope (acceleration) is largest at first and falls to zero as she reaches a steady top speed.
options: A constant acceleration would give a straight v-t line, not a curve.
The graph still rises, so her velocity keeps increasing, just more slowly.
A steeper slope would mean more acceleration; this slope gets gentler.
Right: the slope of the v-t graph is the acceleration, and the slope shrinks to zero.

items.q: An acceleration-time graph for a cart is a horizontal line at +0.40 m/s² from t = 0 to t = 5.0 s. The cart's velocity at t = 0 is +0.30 m/s. What is its velocity at t = 5.0 s?

mistakes.why: Value: 2.0 m/s is the change in velocity (the area). Add the starting velocity, 0.30 m/s.
Value: under a horizontal line the area is a rectangle, height × width, with no ½.

why.correct: The area under the a-t graph is the change in velocity: Δv = (0.40 m/s²)(5.0 s) = 2.0 m/s. v = 0.30 m/s + 2.0 m/s = 2.3 m/s.

items.q: A motion diagram shows a cart's positions at equal time intervals. The dots get closer together from left to right while the cart moves right. What are the directions of its velocity and acceleration?
options: Velocity to the right, acceleration to the right
Velocity to the right, acceleration to the left
Velocity to the left, acceleration to the left
Velocity to the right, zero acceleration

why.correct: Spacing shows speed: bigger gaps mean faster. Shrinking gaps while moving right mean v right and a left.
options: That would make the gaps grow: speeding up.
Right: it moves right, and shrinking gaps mean it is slowing, so a points opposite to v.
The cart moves right, so its velocity points right.
Zero acceleration would give equal gaps.

items.q: A ball is dropped from rest off a bridge. Air resistance is negligible. Predict how each quantity changes from 1.0 s after release to 2.0 s after release.

variables.name: Its speed
variables.why: v = gt grows: 9.8 m/s at 1.0 s, 19.6 m/s at 2.0 s.

variables.name: Its acceleration
variables.why: In free fall the acceleration is g at every instant, so it stays 9.8 m/s² downward.

variables.name: The distance it falls in each 0.10 s
variables.why: It is moving faster, so each 0.10 s covers more distance: the strobe images spread out.

why.correct: Free fall: constant acceleration g, so the velocity grows steadily and the gaps between equal-time images grow.
